evals.name: prefer-native-over-ocr
evals.prompt: I have a screenshot of a PDF page I want to feed to the model. Should I just OCR the screenshot?
evals.expected_output: Asks whether the original PDF is available instead of the screenshot, and if it has a real text layer, recommends extracting text directly from the PDF rather than OCR-ing a screenshot of it -- explaining that a screenshot is a lossy re-encoding of content that may already be natively digital, so OCR-ing it is an avoidable accuracy and token cost.

assertions.text: Asks whether the original PDF (rather than the screenshot) is available
Recommends checking for a native text layer in the PDF before defaulting to OCR
Explains that OCR-ing a screenshot of already-digital content is an avoidable source of error/cost compared to native extraction
Does not simply agree to OCR the screenshot without raising the native-source alternative

evals.name: table-serialization-token-choice
evals.prompt: I scraped an HTML table with 500 rows of sales data and want to paste the raw HTML into the prompt. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: Recommends against pasting raw HTML for tabular data, explaining that a format like CSV/TSV would represent the same information far more token-efficiently than repeated HTML tags per cell, and proposes converting the table to CSV (or a similarly compact structured format) before including it, rather than approving the raw HTML paste.

assertions.text: Recommends against including the raw HTML table as-is due to token inefficiency
Proposes a more compact serialization (e.g. CSV/TSV) as the alternative
Explains the reasoning (repeated tags/markup per cell cost tokens without adding information) rather than just asserting it's inefficient
Does not simply approve pasting the raw 500-row HTML table

evals.name: low-confidence-ocr-flagging
evals.prompt: I ran OCR on a scanned invoice and it extracted the total as '$1,2OO.00' -- the O's look like they might actually be zeros. Should I just go with what OCR gave me?
evals.expected_output: Flags this as a high-stakes value (a monetary amount) that should be spot-checked against the original image rather than trusted as-is, given the visible ambiguity between 'O' and '0', and recommends verifying or clearly flagging the uncertainty rather than silently passing '$1,2OO.00' through as a reliable value.

assertions.text: Identifies the monetary amount as a high-stakes value warranting verification rather than blind trust in the OCR output
Does not recommend simply accepting '$1,2OO.00' as-is without flagging the ambiguity
Recommends either verifying against the original image or explicitly flagging the uncertainty in the output
Treats this as a concrete example of a low-confidence extraction requiring explicit handling, not a minor detail

evals.name: dont-summarize-critical-content
evals.prompt: This 40-page contract is too long for our context budget. Let's just summarize the whole thing into a couple of paragraphs before sending it to the model for a compliance check.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on blanket summarization for a compliance-check task, explaining that summarizing away specific clauses/terms would defeat the purpose of a task that depends on exact contractual language, and recommends alternatives like retrieving only the relevant sections/clauses for the specific compliance question, or clearly distinguishing which parts (e.g. boilerplate) are safe to condense from which parts (specific obligations, terms, dates) must be preserved verbatim.

assertions.text: Pushes back on blanket summarization of the entire contract given the task is a compliance check that likely depends on exact language
Distinguishes between content safe to condense (boilerplate) and content that must be preserved verbatim (specific clauses/terms/obligations)
Proposes an alternative such as retrieving only the relevant sections rather than summarizing everything
Does not simply agree to summarize the whole 40-page contract into a couple of paragraphs

evals.name: boilerplate-vs-content-distinction
evals.prompt: This scraped documentation site has the same sidebar navigation and footer repeated on every one of the 30 pages I extracted. Can we just strip all repeated-looking text to save tokens?
evals.expected_output: Agrees that the repeated navigation/footer boilerplate should be stripped or deduplicated, but cautions against stripping 'all repeated-looking text' indiscriminately, since some legitimately repeated content (e.g. a recurring code pattern, a standard warning notice that varies slightly per page, or similar-looking headings with different content) could be mistaken for boilerplate and wrongly removed -- recommends verifying what's actually identical/non-informational before stripping rather than a blanket repeated-text filter.

assertions.text: Agrees that genuine boilerplate (repeated nav/footer) is safe to strip or deduplicate
Cautions against a blanket 'strip all repeated-looking text' rule, since some repeated-looking content may still be informational and differ page to page
Recommends checking that stripped content is actually identical/non-informational rather than assuming anything that looks repeated is boilerplate
Does not simply approve an indiscriminate repeated-text filter without this caveat
